full_text:
Interviewer:	Ok, are you going on a placement?

Subject:	Yes

Interviewer:	Ok then, I’ll tell you a bit about what we’re doing then. The project that we’re looking at, is mainly looking at engineers, well female engineers. We’ve decided to include design and technology students, partly because we’re also doing the study at [name] University and they include design and technology under their engineering more than at [this university] and also because the reason we’re looking at it is because engineering is a male dominated environment, which I think design and technology is as well. But the project that we’re doing is looking at women’s experiences of education so far and their expectations of the placement and why they want to do a placement. So if its alright with you, I’ll just start off asking you a few background questions, like why you’ve decided to do design and technology. Ok? What ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	Design and technology, geography and business studies.

Interviewer:	Ok, what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	Just a normal community college.

Interviewer:	It wasn’t?

Subject:	Private or anything? No.

Interviewer:	Have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, well not proper. In January I did some work for my landlord, doing graphic design and stuff for him, but not like proper employed work.

Interviewer:	Ok, what do your parents do? Are either of them in the industry at all?

Subject:	No my mum’s an occupational therapist and my dad’s a computer programmer.

Interviewer:	So when and why do you think that you decided to design and technology?

Subject:	Erm, well when I was at school it was just the easiest subject for me, and so it was sort of the natural thing to go and do it at university. It was a bit of a hard decision because a lot of the design and technology courses, you have to have an art foundation, but erm this one you didn’t so.

Interviewer:	Did you have much careers advice or anything like that when you was at school?

Subject:	Erm, not – you could get careers advice but it was absolutely useless, so I didn’t really bother.

Interviewer:	Ok, have your family been supportive about the decision to do design?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Ok, did you do much career research yourself, like looking into what’s involved in design and technology?

Subject:	Not at all, I probably should have done some. I wasn’t sure what I wanted to study and basically my mum was looking at courses for me really because I couldn’t be bothered, which is awful. But erm, she was looking. And I didn’t, because I had to come to an interview here, I found that a bit more (encouraging?) because I didn’t know before I came what it was going to be like so if I hadn’t had an interview I probably wouldn’t have much of an idea.

Interviewer:	What do you think it is that appeals to you about design and technology then?

Subject:	Erm, its just that its not just sitting around learning. You’re making things as well, its much more of a sociable course than other ones. Like we, I know everyone on the course because we’re always making things, we’re never just sat in a lecture theatre, we’re always doing something, which makes it much more interesting. 

Interviewer:	Did you ever consider studying any other subjects?

Subject:	Since my ‘A’ level results, I thought I should have done geography, but I never really thought of it before. I always thought I’d do design really. But I’m not necessarily interested in doing it after I’ve finished university. Its just something I’m doing at the moment really.

Interviewer:	That’s interesting. When you started looking at courses, or when you decided to come to [this university], did you know that you wanted to do the sandwich course?

Subject:	Yes, I’ve always wanted to because I thought I wanted to spend more than 3 years at university and it’d be quite a good experience but I wasn’t sure if I’d get one, because its quite hard to get one. But I have now so, that’s a relief. 

Interviewer:	How did you decide to come to [this university] then?

Subject:	Well I went to open days for quite a few universities and this is one of the places I liked the most – I was impressed when I came along. I think I actually came to 2 open days, because I came to the first one and thought I liked it quite a lot, so I came to another one just to make sure. Yes, that’s why I decided.

Interviewer:	When you decided to do design and technology, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Subject:	Erm, yes, I knew it was. Well all of the courses I had interviews, it was always an issue, when I went to the interview I could tell, like a lot of the people interviewing me, particularly at other universities, they were desperate to get me on the course because they needed to balance out their numbers. I’ve always felt like I don’t know if I would have got on this course if I’d been a bloke. My interview wasn’t particularly design orientated, they weren’t really looking at my work, we were just chatting about my CV and what I did out of time, and I wasn’t really, I sort of thought I wasn’t going to be accepted whatever because, to make up their numbers.

Interviewer:	Ok that’s interesting, did that sort of attitude bother you at all then?

Subject:	It does bother me a bit because they, there’s certain things you need to be good at to be on this course, and the interviews, the reason the interview is there, is so they can make sure you’re going to be capable of doing things. But they didn’t even look at my work, so they couldn’t have know, and every bloke I’ve spoken to had a really vigorous interview. They remember them now, they were really grilled and my interview was, we talked about scuba diving which I’ve never even done. He got his holiday photos out and I mean, luckily I’ve been able to cope with it, but if I hadn’t been capable, it could have put me in quite a lot of trouble when I got here, if I wasn’t able to handle it. Other places as well, I went to an interview at [university] and they haven’t enough girls on their course. They have like 6 on average a year out of about 300, and their course is like renowned for being an arty course, and I’m not an arty person, but they never even looked at my work, and if I’d gone there I definitely would have found it really hard but luckily I just knew about the course, so I got (in touch?) anyway, it was a bit …

Interviewer:	Is that what other girls on your course have experienced as well?

Subject:	Erm I think so yes. Its just, there are more women than I thought there would be, I think there’s about 20 of us out of 130, which I suppose isn’t too bad, but I think everyone, out of all the girls (lost words)

Interviewer:	That’s really interesting. So apart from that side of it, did it bother you that there were going to be so few girls on the course?

Subject:	No, it didn’t bother me at all. I mean it was the same at school, there wasn’t many girls in our design group and if anything I got preferential treatment so it didn’t really bother me.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design and technology?

Subject:	Yes I do, I don’t see why not, but erm I suppose its just what people want to do. I just don’t think it’s a particularly girly thing to do, going and standing in a machine shop and cutting up bits of metal, I just don’t think many girls want to do it really. But they should be encouraged to.

Interviewer:	Do you think that girls are given enough opportunity and enough information about the subject to make a reasonable decision not to take it?

Subject:	Yes erm, I don’t know. Once I’d decided on a few courses, I got sent a load of literature from the courses about girls doing engineering and stuff and about grants that are available and. So once I’d applied there was a lot of information, but you had to apply first to get it. It depends as well how designs conducted at your school, we only did like technology, so engineering, I don’t think anyone knew much about engineering really, it just depends like how you’re taught really. I just didn’t even think about engineering, I didn’t know what it was so it wasn’t really an option.

Interviewer:	Ok, what do you think could be done to encourage more women, or even more men, into the industry?

Subject:	Well maybe, a few courses do like poster schemes in schools, and like there are a lot of grants available for women to do engineering. I mean I got a load of stuff about quite a few of them, so if they actually advertised them, it’d be like an incentive. Because people go into teaching because of the grants and stuff you get for that so, and that was advertised, so maybe they should do the same for engineering.

Interviewer:	Ok, what characteristics do you think make a good designer?

Subject:	Er, well being able to draws quite important, but being like, kind of all round, like, because we do quite a lot of technology as well, whereas a lot of courses are just into making things look pretty, but you need to be able to have things work as well, so its quite important to be good at like maths and physics as well as art.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male characteristics or female characteristics?

Subject:	Erm, I suppose, I would say that art is more of a girly thing, I don’t know why I think that I just would, and maybe the sciences are more of a male thing, but in this course you seem to get more males doing it, I don’t know why. I suppose girls are supposed to be more academic and you don’t have to get good grades to do the course, its more to do with initiative and doing things yourself, which might attract more males.

Interviewer:	You’ve said a bit about this already, but what do you think are the advantages of being a woman in a male dominated environment?

Subject:	I think you do get preferential treatment, erm we have like, our technicians are more inclined to help the girls in workshops and stuff. But on the downside you’re in a minority, being a minority, if you have like group projects or somethings, you’re likely to get shouted down or you’ve got to be quite strong-minded person to get your views across and stuff, but the main advantage is extra help and people, and like I think there probably is more chance of getting a job afterwards. Like coming to university they were trying to balance out their numbers and…

Interviewer:	Has the course then been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Erm, I didn’t know much about it to be honest before I came, but it was harder than I thought it would be, I did struggle at first doing my work, but I’m settled into it now and its good. I’m mean I like working hard, I’m used to it now and I get bored if I don’t have designs to do and stuff, so yeah its alright.

Interviewer:	What would you say are the best and the worst things so far?

Subject:	Er, I like the making, making things, but I’m not so keen, just the amount of coursework that we get is phenomenal (lost words) it’s like we’ve got to hand in 6 pieces of course work and an exam in 2 days during, at the end of July, is going to be a bit of a nightmare, but you’ve just got to work out how you’re going to deal with them.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you had any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	Yes. We’ve got quite a few actually. Erm my (disable?) lecturer is female. I hadn’t ever really thought about it.

Interviewer:	Have you noticed any differences in the type of subject that the women teach or their style of teaching?

Subject:	Erm, she’s left now but we had, she was head of, she was head of one of our modules and she did a lot of stuff on like user focused design, she also wasn’t so much of the technical side of things, and the other female lecturer that I’ve got is more environmental design, but they’re not the main design areas.

Interviewer:	Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	I don’t think so. I’ve never really noticed whether they’re male or female.

Interviewer:	Ok do the female lecturers treat you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Yes, I suppose they do. But they’re more, the male, I think the only time I’m treated differently by the male lecturers is like in labs or in workshops where the female lecturers don’t teach us, so I can’t really say whether they treat us differently or not.

Interviewer:	What about the male lecturers, do they treat they female and the male students the same?

Subject:	I think they do, because there’s quite a lot of other people on our course, when you’re in a big group, I think you treat everyone the same, so I don’t think there’s an issue there.

Interviewer:	Have you got a personal tutor? (yes) Are they male as well? (yes) Would you rather have a female personal tutor or doesn’t it bother you?

Subject:	He is actually a really nice tutor, he’s so nice to me. So I’m not bothered, but I know other, my friends some of them have got nasty tutors, but I don’t know if that’s because they’re male. I don’t think male or female makes a difference, its just the type of person you have.

Interviewer:	Is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know, I mean my tutor’s (?), he’s just really nice to me. He just takes a genuine interest in what you’re doing the whole time, a lot, he’s always sending emails going y’know pop in and tell me what you’re up to and things like that, and its nice to know that someone’s sort of looking out for you, but I don’t know if that’s really an influence.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you have to do quite a lot of group work on your course then?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Do you like doing group work?

Subject:	Yes I do. There’s sort of pros and cons. We’re just starting a group project now and er, like today we’re supposed to be doing some machining, but there’s 4 of us, and there’s no time in the day when all 4 of us are free and no-one wants to go and do it themselves because they want everyone to pull their weight, but there’s no time when everyone’s free, so it’s a bit of organisational stuff. But erm, yes its alright, in fact this group, there’s 2 girls and 2 boys so everything’s quite even really.

Interviewer:	Do you find that there is a difference between working with men and women?

Subject:	Erm, it just nice, it is nice to have, maybe if I was with 3 boys in my group, I might have felt a little bit over- y’know a little bit at the bottom of the scales. But its nice …

Interviewer:	Do you think that you feel like that because of how they treat you or is that just something … ?

Subject:	I don’t know its probably just me actually, I probably just feel a bit intimidated, I don’t think it’s the way they treat you, but then a lot of the work is sort of typical man work with machines, and they just don’t expect you to be able to do it, and they’re probably right, they probably are better at it than me.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think there’s any aspects of the teaching or advice that you’ve had that will help you on your placement?

Subject:	Erm, well out of the, a lot of the placements aren’t really that related to the course. I think mine is quite related, its supposed to be like packaging design, but its hard to know exactly what I’ll be doing. Like, there has been a lot of just, there have been a few lectures on getting your portfolio together and how you can get a job, but my personal tutor’s has looked over all my application forms and stuff before I sent them off. Erm, so I think that everything, I mean everything that I’ve done has taught me something, so it should help me out, but I don’t really know what I’ll be doing, so I don’t – I’m supposed to be doing the packaging and design side, but I don’t know how much input I’ll actually get, whether I’ll just be sort of a trainee watching what goes on?

Interviewer:	What do you think are the main skills that you’ll take from the course?

Subject:	Organisations probably the main thing, the biggest, just getting things done on time and going places on time. Because we have so much on at once, you have to make sure everything’s organised and stuff – I think that’ll be the main thing I take. And yes, just a little bit of everything really.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’ll be more of the technical things or do you think it’ll be things like group work and that?

Subject:	I think it might be, yeah, all the group work and stuff less than the technical things. Like I will do quite a lot of CAD and stuff, but at the end of the day (lost words) its going to be entirely different.

Interviewer:	Do you feel prepared and ready to go on the placement now?

Subject:	Yes, I went to see my manager last week, so I’ve seen where I’ll be and all the offices, and met her, so it kind of put my mind at rest because it was a bit of an unknown. And next week we’ve got like a welcome day, where we meet all the other placement students, and that, so I’m quite happy about it really. I think they’ve done quite a lot to make sure we feel happy before we go there sort of thing, so.

Interviewer:	Why did you really decide to go on placement then?

Subject:	Because, it’ll be nice to work for a year rather than studying. I think I’m too, I don’t feel old enough to do my final year or prepared enough. I’m just not ready to take on all the work really, I want to stall for a year. Its quite nice because we’ve done 2 years of work and the final year’s going to be quite a lot of work, so its quite nice to have a sort of break in the middle. Its interesting to see what it’ll be like in the workplace.

Interviewer:	Do you think when you come back to uni, you’ll bring anything back from the workplace to help you?

Subject:	I hope so, I don’t know whether it will or not, but its worth a go. I hope it will, its supposed to. Often we get told we need to do a placement because it’ll help you do your final year and hopefully get some ideas for my final project and stuff, but as I said, I don’t really know what I’ll be doing.

Interviewer:	Who is the company that you’re going to work for?

Subject:	 [company]

Interviewer:	Ok, what attracted you to them?

Subject:	Well they came here (??) they came and gave a presentation in our department about the job, because the girl who’s doing a placement at the moment’s on our course as well, so she said, she told the company she’d like to come and talk to us, and erm, its just a online application form, I didn’t really look at what the job was, but erm I got offered an interview so I went along and they really impressed me on the day. I just felt that I really wanted it, so I was quite pleased actually.

Interviewer:	Did you look at anything like location, training opportunities, and what prospects you might have when you leave?

Subject:	Erm, I knew it would be quite hard to get a job, so I wasn’t trying to think about location. I sort of said to myself I’d go anywhere, but luckily its just down the road from here so its ideal really, although I said I’d go anywhere, its much nicer to be near here and be where all my friends will be next year. Erm, and I didn’t really look at training and stuff, but since I’ve spoken to the manager, there is quite a lot on offer, and that’s definitely, I mean I’m definitely going to accept the job, like they’ve impressed me that they’ve told me what, there are a lot of opportunities for me to further myself and things so.

Interviewer:	How many other placement students do they take?

Subject:	There’s 50 but there different sites, I think there’s about 6 or 7 going to Melton, at our site.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that that will help you as well?

Subject:	Oh definitely yes. A lot of them are on my course as well, so I know them all already. And I get to meet some more of them next week, we’re meeting them all, so erm, it’ll be really nice just to have other people who are in the same sort of situation being around, it won’t feel quite so daunting.

Interviewer:	Do you know anything about the gender proportions in the company?

Subject:	I don’t, but as far as – I went to visit, and my manager’s female, the girl who’s on placement already’s female, and I think there was 3, in like the little department there was 3 girls and 3 blokes, so I think it was quite even really.

Interviewer:	Did you ever have the option to get a sponsorship?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think there would have been any advantages or disadvantages to being sponsored?

Subject:	Erm, if I’d had the opportunity I would probably have gone for it, but I know that if you are sponsored you’re kind of tied down a little bit so, I’m not really bothered that I’m not in that position. Sometimes companies sponsor you in the final year but that sort of ties you down, if, I’m not really that bothered, but then if I’m doing the placement it should pay for my final year work.

Interviewer:	What are you most looking forward to about the placement?

Subject:	Just the independence really. Mostly the fact that I’ll be able to buy a car. Just, I’ve always done little odd jobs at different places, but it’ll be nice to do like a proper job for a bit.

Interviewer:	And what are you most apprehensive about?

Subject:	Being able to do the work, that you have the ability to do the work. I don’t know what its going to be, and I don’t want to feel like I can’t do it, but they have, (I felt like it was the same with this course?), and I feel like they’ve found out about me enough and they should know whether I’d be capable, so hopefully I’ll be ok.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there’s anything else that the university could do to help prepare you?

Subject:	Erm, I think for my placement they did, because they take on a lot of placement students and they’re used to it, if it was a smaller company I probably wouldn’t know quite so much about it, about what its going to be like and stuff, but as I’m with quite a large company, I’m ok really, they’ve set us up quite well.

Interviewer:	How do you expect work to differ from being at university?

Subject:	Erm. Its going to be, I know its going to be working sort of solid through 9 til 5, but then there’s not going to be any work once we finish so. Whereas here there’s no real obligation to do that much in the day, but there’s always something on your mind, there’s always some piece of coursework that needs doing or something, so its going to be quite different, like you can switch off at 5 o’clock and not think about it until the next day, so its going to be quite interesting.

Interviewer:	In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

Subject:	Its probably going to be quite a telling year this year, whether I like it or not. I mean, like I said it was natural for me to come and do design because it was the easiest thing for me, but I don’t know if I want to do it for the rest of my life, or even straight after university. Erm, I’ll wait and see how much I enjoy next year.

Interviewer:	Do you think that will play a part in helping you make your mind up?

Subject:	Yeah, definitely. If I enjoy next year, then I might, y’know, I might go for the same company’s graduate scheme and stuff or I might just decide to do something totally different.

Interviewer:	Ok, what would be your ideal career then?

Subject:	I would quite like to be sort of managerial. I quite like sort of office work, which isn’t really particularly designy. That’s why I sort of think that there’s offices side of design as well so I think that’s why its going to be quite interesting this year, ‘cos I think I’ll be doing more of that kind of thing so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll encounter any difficulties trying to achieve like your ideal career?

Subject:	Yeah probably because if it isn’t related to design, I won’t have done a related degree. But hopefully just by doing a placement and having the work experience, it’ll help me get whatever I decide I want to do, but I’m not even entirely sure what I want to do so.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that if you do go into the industry the career prospects are good?

Subject:	No I don’t think they are. I know its quite hard to erm, as far as I can see the design and technology industry is struggling, unless you’re really good. You either a flyer or you’re struggling. And I think (lost words) I’ve become complacent and all of them, they can’t tell what their financial climate’s going to be from year to year. So I don’t think its that easy unless you get involved with a big company, its definitely hard to have your own little design company.

Interviewer:	Does that worry you at all?

Subject:	No because I’m not particularly interested in doing it anyway. If I was interested it would worry me, but erm I’m not really bothered whether I do it or not so.

Interviewer:	Ok are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made so far? Or would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

Subject:	I probably, I don’t know if I would’ve took my course. I found it really hard in the first few months, but I’m not the kind of person who sort of drops out. I think I’m a bit of a perseverer. So erm, I sort of decided that this is something, I’ll feel really prod of myself once I finished it because it is hard work. It’d be easy just to say oh I’d rather do something a bit easier, but erm yes. I don’t actually, I don’t regret it at all really. I think its good for me, and whatever I’m meant to do I’ll do sort of thing.

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics or the culture of the design and technology industry?

Subject:	Oh I’ve got no idea. The culture of it? (yeah) What does that sort of mean?

Interviewer:	Like the characteristics, like descriptive words really like competitive

Subject:	So yes, its competitive (pause).

Interviewer:	Would you use masculine as a word to describe it?

Subject:	Erm yes probably.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that it is so masculine? Do you think it is just due to the numbers of males?

Subject:	Yes I think so, its just due to the imbalance and its not just the industry its everywhere, it sort of makes you think its not just a one off, there is a massive imbalance.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the situation will improve at all?

Subject:	Em, yeah I think so, I hope so. I think its just grad – slowly improving. I mean there’s certainly more girls on my course than I was told there would be when I had the interview. And I know there’s more, because there’s more opportunities, I mean there’s a shortage of design teachers anyway, but like female (lost words) more advantages and more likely to get a job so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any aspects of the culture, or the fact that its so masculine might cause you any problems at all?

Subject:	No I don’t think so, you’ve got to be, you’ve just got to be quite a strong person. I mean if you were quite quiet and sort of retiring you could find it more intimidating that you’ve got to take on – and in fact, probably, its probably quite daunting for the males, is the females coming in saying, well laying out what they want to do, so you’ve got to turn it round really.

Interviewer:	Ok that’s everything thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Design and technology, geography and business studies.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Just a normal community college.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It wasn’t?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Private or anything? No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well not proper. In January I did some work for my landlord, doing graphic design and stuff for him, but not like proper employed work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what do your parents do? Are either of them in the industry at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No my mum’s an occupational therapist and my dad’s a computer programmer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So when and why do you think that you decided to design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well when I was at school it was just the easiest subject for me, and so it was sort of the natural thing to go and do it at university. It was a bit of a hard decision because a lot of the design and technology courses, you have to have an art foundation, but erm this one you didn’t so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have much careers advice or anything like that when you was at school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not – you could get careers advice but it was absolutely useless, so I didn’t really bother.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have your family been supportive about the decision to do design?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, did you do much career research yourself, like looking into what’s involved in design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not at all, I probably should have done some. I wasn’t sure what I wanted to study and basically my mum was looking at courses for me really because I couldn’t be bothered, which is awful. But erm, she was looking. And I didn’t, because I had to come to an interview here, I found that a bit more (encouraging?) because I didn’t know before I came what it was going to be like so if I hadn’t had an interview I probably wouldn’t have much of an idea.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think it is that appeals to you about design and technology then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, its just that its not just sitting around learning. You’re making things as well, its much more of a sociable course than other ones. Like we, I know everyone on the course because we’re always making things, we’re never just sat in a lecture theatre, we’re always doing something, which makes it much more interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you ever consider studying any other subjects?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Since my ‘A’ level results, I thought I should have done geography, but I never really thought of it before. I always thought I’d do design really. But I’m not necessarily interested in doing it after I’ve finished university. Its just something I’m doing at the moment really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s interesting. When you started looking at courses, or when you decided to come to [this university], did you know that you wanted to do the sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I’ve always wanted to because I thought I wanted to spend more than 3 years at university and it’d be quite a good experience but I wasn’t sure if I’d get one, because its quite hard to get one. But I have now so, that’s a relief.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you decide to come to [this university] then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well I went to open days for quite a few universities and this is one of the places I liked the most – I was impressed when I came along. I think I actually came to 2 open days, because I came to the first one and thought I liked it quite a lot, so I came to another one just to make sure. Yes, that’s why I decided.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you decided to do design and technology, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yes, I knew it was. Well all of the courses I had interviews, it was always an issue, when I went to the interview I could tell, like a lot of the people interviewing me, particularly at other universities, they were desperate to get me on the course because they needed to balance out their numbers. I’ve always felt like I don’t know if I would have got on this course if I’d been a bloke. My interview wasn’t particularly design orientated, they weren’t really looking at my work, we were just chatting about my CV and what I did out of time, and I wasn’t really, I sort of thought I wasn’t going to be accepted whatever because, to make up their numbers.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok that’s interesting, did that sort of attitude bother you at all then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It does bother me a bit because they, there’s certain things you need to be good at to be on this course, and the interviews, the reason the interview is there, is so they can make sure you’re going to be capable of doing things. But they didn’t even look at my work, so they couldn’t have know, and every bloke I’ve spoken to had a really vigorous interview. They remember them now, they were really grilled and my interview was, we talked about scuba diving which I’ve never even done. He got his holiday photos out and I mean, luckily I’ve been able to cope with it, but if I hadn’t been capable, it could have put me in quite a lot of trouble when I got here, if I wasn’t able to handle it. Other places as well, I went to an interview at [university] and they haven’t enough girls on their course. They have like 6 on average a year out of about 300, and their course is like renowned for being an arty course, and I’m not an arty person, but they never even looked at my work, and if I’d gone there I definitely would have found it really hard but luckily I just knew about the course, so I got (in touch?) anyway, it was a bit …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that what other girls on your course have experienced as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm I think so yes. Its just, there are more women than I thought there would be, I think there’s about 20 of us out of 130, which I suppose isn’t too bad, but I think everyone, out of all the girls (lost words)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s really interesting. So apart from that side of it, did it bother you that there were going to be so few girls on the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, it didn’t bother me at all. I mean it was the same at school, there wasn’t many girls in our design group and if anything I got preferential treatment so it didn’t really bother me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design and technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I do, I don’t see why not, but erm I suppose its just what people want to do. I just don’t think it’s a particularly girly thing to do, going and standing in a machine shop and cutting up bits of metal, I just don’t think many girls want to do it really. But they should be encouraged to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that girls are given enough opportunity and enough information about the subject to make a reasonable decision not to take it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes erm, I don’t know. Once I’d decided on a few courses, I got sent a load of literature from the courses about girls doing engineering and stuff and about grants that are available and. So once I’d applied there was a lot of information, but you had to apply first to get it. It depends as well how designs conducted at your school, we only did like technology, so engineering, I don’t think anyone knew much about engineering really, it just depends like how you’re taught really. I just didn’t even think about engineering, I didn’t know what it was so it wasn’t really an option.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what do you think could be done to encourage more women, or even more men, into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well maybe, a few courses do like poster schemes in schools, and like there are a lot of grants available for women to do engineering. I mean I got a load of stuff about quite a few of them, so if they actually advertised them, it’d be like an incentive. Because people go into teaching because of the grants and stuff you get for that so, and that was advertised, so maybe they should do the same for engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what characteristics do you think make a good designer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, well being able to draws quite important, but being like, kind of all round, like, because we do quite a lot of technology as well, whereas a lot of courses are just into making things look pretty, but you need to be able to have things work as well, so its quite important to be good at like maths and physics as well as art.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male characteristics or female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I suppose, I would say that art is more of a girly thing, I don’t know why I think that I just would, and maybe the sciences are more of a male thing, but in this course you seem to get more males doing it, I don’t know why. I suppose girls are supposed to be more academic and you don’t have to get good grades to do the course, its more to do with initiative and doing things yourself, which might attract more males.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’ve said a bit about this already, but what do you think are the advantages of being a woman in a male dominated environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think you do get preferential treatment, erm we have like, our technicians are more inclined to help the girls in workshops and stuff. But on the downside you’re in a minority, being a minority, if you have like group projects or somethings, you’re likely to get shouted down or you’ve got to be quite strong-minded person to get your views across and stuff, but the main advantage is extra help and people, and like I think there probably is more chance of getting a job afterwards. Like coming to university they were trying to balance out their numbers and…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has the course then been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I didn’t know much about it to be honest before I came, but it was harder than I thought it would be, I did struggle at first doing my work, but I’m settled into it now and its good. I’m mean I like working hard, I’m used to it now and I get bored if I don’t have designs to do and stuff, so yeah its alright.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you say are the best and the worst things so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I like the making, making things, but I’m not so keen, just the amount of coursework that we get is phenomenal (lost words) it’s like we’ve got to hand in 6 pieces of course work and an exam in 2 days during, at the end of July, is going to be a bit of a nightmare, but you’ve just got to work out how you’re going to deal with them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you had any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. We’ve got quite a few actually. Erm my (disable?) lecturer is female. I hadn’t ever really thought about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you noticed any differences in the type of subject that the women teach or their style of teaching?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, she’s left now but we had, she was head of, she was head of one of our modules and she did a lot of stuff on like user focused design, she also wasn’t so much of the technical side of things, and the other female lecturer that I’ve got is more environmental design, but they’re not the main design areas.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think so. I’ve never really noticed whether they’re male or female.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok do the female lecturers treat you the same as the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I suppose they do. But they’re more, the male, I think the only time I’m treated differently by the male lecturers is like in labs or in workshops where the female lecturers don’t teach us, so I can’t really say whether they treat us differently or not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about the male lecturers, do they treat they female and the male students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think they do, because there’s quite a lot of other people on our course, when you’re in a big group, I think you treat everyone the same, so I don’t think there’s an issue there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you got a personal tutor? (yes) Are they male as well? (yes) Would you rather have a female personal tutor or doesn’t it bother you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He is actually a really nice tutor, he’s so nice to me. So I’m not bothered, but I know other, my friends some of them have got nasty tutors, but I don’t know if that’s because they’re male. I don’t think male or female makes a difference, its just the type of person you have.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything or anyone that you would say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know, I mean my tutor’s (?), he’s just really nice to me. He just takes a genuine interest in what you’re doing the whole time, a lot, he’s always sending emails going y’know pop in and tell me what you’re up to and things like that, and its nice to know that someone’s sort of looking out for you, but I don’t know if that’s really an influence.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you have to do quite a lot of group work on your course then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you like doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I do. There’s sort of pros and cons. We’re just starting a group project now and er, like today we’re supposed to be doing some machining, but there’s 4 of us, and there’s no time in the day when all 4 of us are free and no-one wants to go and do it themselves because they want everyone to pull their weight, but there’s no time when everyone’s free, so it’s a bit of organisational stuff. But erm, yes its alright, in fact this group, there’s 2 girls and 2 boys so everything’s quite even really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find that there is a difference between working with men and women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it just nice, it is nice to have, maybe if I was with 3 boys in my group, I might have felt a little bit over- y’know a little bit at the bottom of the scales. But its nice …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you feel like that because of how they treat you or is that just something … ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know its probably just me actually, I probably just feel a bit intimidated, I don’t think it’s the way they treat you, but then a lot of the work is sort of typical man work with machines, and they just don’t expect you to be able to do it, and they’re probably right, they probably are better at it than me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think there’s any aspects of the teaching or advice that you’ve had that will help you on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well out of the, a lot of the placements aren’t really that related to the course. I think mine is quite related, its supposed to be like packaging design, but its hard to know exactly what I’ll be doing. Like, there has been a lot of just, there have been a few lectures on getting your portfolio together and how you can get a job, but my personal tutor’s has looked over all my application forms and stuff before I sent them off. Erm, so I think that everything, I mean everything that I’ve done has taught me something, so it should help me out, but I don’t really know what I’ll be doing, so I don’t – I’m supposed to be doing the packaging and design side, but I don’t know how much input I’ll actually get, whether I’ll just be sort of a trainee watching what goes on?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the main skills that you’ll take from the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Organisations probably the main thing, the biggest, just getting things done on time and going places on time. Because we have so much on at once, you have to make sure everything’s organised and stuff – I think that’ll be the main thing I take. And yes, just a little bit of everything really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’ll be more of the technical things or do you think it’ll be things like group work and that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it might be, yeah, all the group work and stuff less than the technical things. Like I will do quite a lot of CAD and stuff, but at the end of the day (lost words) its going to be entirely different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel prepared and ready to go on the placement now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I went to see my manager last week, so I’ve seen where I’ll be and all the offices, and met her, so it kind of put my mind at rest because it was a bit of an unknown. And next week we’ve got like a welcome day, where we meet all the other placement students, and that, so I’m quite happy about it really. I think they’ve done quite a lot to make sure we feel happy before we go there sort of thing, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why did you really decide to go on placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because, it’ll be nice to work for a year rather than studying. I think I’m too, I don’t feel old enough to do my final year or prepared enough. I’m just not ready to take on all the work really, I want to stall for a year. Its quite nice because we’ve done 2 years of work and the final year’s going to be quite a lot of work, so its quite nice to have a sort of break in the middle. Its interesting to see what it’ll be like in the workplace.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think when you come back to uni, you’ll bring anything back from the workplace to help you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope so, I don’t know whether it will or not, but its worth a go. I hope it will, its supposed to. Often we get told we need to do a placement because it’ll help you do your final year and hopefully get some ideas for my final project and stuff, but as I said, I don’t really know what I’ll be doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Who is the company that you’re going to work for?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [company]

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what attracted you to them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well they came here (??) they came and gave a presentation in our department about the job, because the girl who’s doing a placement at the moment’s on our course as well, so she said, she told the company she’d like to come and talk to us, and erm, its just a online application form, I didn’t really look at what the job was, but erm I got offered an interview so I went along and they really impressed me on the day. I just felt that I really wanted it, so I was quite pleased actually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you look at anything like location, training opportunities, and what prospects you might have when you leave?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I knew it would be quite hard to get a job, so I wasn’t trying to think about location. I sort of said to myself I’d go anywhere, but luckily its just down the road from here so its ideal really, although I said I’d go anywhere, its much nicer to be near here and be where all my friends will be next year. Erm, and I didn’t really look at training and stuff, but since I’ve spoken to the manager, there is quite a lot on offer, and that’s definitely, I mean I’m definitely going to accept the job, like they’ve impressed me that they’ve told me what, there are a lot of opportunities for me to further myself and things so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many other placement students do they take?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There’s 50 but there different sites, I think there’s about 6 or 7 going to Melton, at our site.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that that will help you as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh definitely yes. A lot of them are on my course as well, so I know them all already. And I get to meet some more of them next week, we’re meeting them all, so erm, it’ll be really nice just to have other people who are in the same sort of situation being around, it won’t feel quite so daunting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know anything about the gender proportions in the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t, but as far as – I went to visit, and my manager’s female, the girl who’s on placement already’s female, and I think there was 3, in like the little department there was 3 girls and 3 blokes, so I think it was quite even really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you ever have the option to get a sponsorship?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think there would have been any advantages or disadvantages to being sponsored?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, if I’d had the opportunity I would probably have gone for it, but I know that if you are sponsored you’re kind of tied down a little bit so, I’m not really bothered that I’m not in that position. Sometimes companies sponsor you in the final year but that sort of ties you down, if, I’m not really that bothered, but then if I’m doing the placement it should pay for my final year work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What are you most looking forward to about the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Just the independence really. Mostly the fact that I’ll be able to buy a car. Just, I’ve always done little odd jobs at different places, but it’ll be nice to do like a proper job for a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what are you most apprehensive about?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Being able to do the work, that you have the ability to do the work. I don’t know what its going to be, and I don’t want to feel like I can’t do it, but they have, (I felt like it was the same with this course?), and I feel like they’ve found out about me enough and they should know whether I’d be capable, so hopefully I’ll be ok.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there’s anything else that the university could do to help prepare you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think for my placement they did, because they take on a lot of placement students and they’re used to it, if it was a smaller company I probably wouldn’t know quite so much about it, about what its going to be like and stuff, but as I’m with quite a large company, I’m ok really, they’ve set us up quite well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you expect work to differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm. Its going to be, I know its going to be working sort of solid through 9 til 5, but then there’s not going to be any work once we finish so. Whereas here there’s no real obligation to do that much in the day, but there’s always something on your mind, there’s always some piece of coursework that needs doing or something, so its going to be quite different, like you can switch off at 5 o’clock and not think about it until the next day, so its going to be quite interesting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In terms of your career then, where do you see yourself in 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Its probably going to be quite a telling year this year, whether I like it or not. I mean, like I said it was natural for me to come and do design because it was the easiest thing for me, but I don’t know if I want to do it for the rest of my life, or even straight after university. Erm, I’ll wait and see how much I enjoy next year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that will play a part in helping you make your mind up?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, definitely. If I enjoy next year, then I might, y’know, I might go for the same company’s graduate scheme and stuff or I might just decide to do something totally different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, what would be your ideal career then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would quite like to be sort of managerial. I quite like sort of office work, which isn’t really particularly designy. That’s why I sort of think that there’s offices side of design as well so I think that’s why its going to be quite interesting this year, ‘cos I think I’ll be doing more of that kind of thing so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ll encounter any difficulties trying to achieve like your ideal career?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah probably because if it isn’t related to design, I won’t have done a related degree. But hopefully just by doing a placement and having the work experience, it’ll help me get whatever I decide I want to do, but I’m not even entirely sure what I want to do so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you think that if you do go into the industry the career prospects are good?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I don’t think they are. I know its quite hard to erm, as far as I can see the design and technology industry is struggling, unless you’re really good. You either a flyer or you’re struggling. And I think (lost words) I’ve become complacent and all of them, they can’t tell what their financial climate’s going to be from year to year. So I don’t think its that easy unless you get involved with a big company, its definitely hard to have your own little design company.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that worry you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No because I’m not particularly interested in doing it anyway. If I was interested it would worry me, but erm I’m not really bothered whether I do it or not so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok are you happy with all the career choices you’ve made so far? Or would you do anything differently if you went through it all again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I probably, I don’t know if I would’ve took my course. I found it really hard in the first few months, but I’m not the kind of person who sort of drops out. I think I’m a bit of a perseverer. So erm, I sort of decided that this is something, I’ll feel really prod of myself once I finished it because it is hard work. It’d be easy just to say oh I’d rather do something a bit easier, but erm yes. I don’t actually, I don’t regret it at all really. I think its good for me, and whatever I’m meant to do I’ll do sort of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics or the culture of the design and technology industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh I’ve got no idea. The culture of it? (yeah) What does that sort of mean?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like the characteristics, like descriptive words really like competitive

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So yes, its competitive (pause).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you use masculine as a word to describe it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm yes probably.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that it is so masculine? Do you think it is just due to the numbers of males?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I think so, its just due to the imbalance and its not just the industry its everywhere, it sort of makes you think its not just a one off, there is a massive imbalance.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the situation will improve at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Em, yeah I think so, I hope so. I think its just grad – slowly improving. I mean there’s certainly more girls on my course than I was told there would be when I had the interview. And I know there’s more, because there’s more opportunities, I mean there’s a shortage of design teachers anyway, but like female (lost words) more advantages and more likely to get a job so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that any aspects of the culture, or the fact that its so masculine might cause you any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I don’t think so, you’ve got to be, you’ve just got to be quite a strong person. I mean if you were quite quiet and sort of retiring you could find it more intimidating that you’ve got to take on – and in fact, probably, its probably quite daunting for the males, is the females coming in saying, well laying out what they want to do, so you’ve got to turn it round really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok that’s everything thank you very much.
